verdict.reasoning: Patient states: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment" and describes "potentially there's a bit of swelling in my lips and tongue. Feels a bit weird" after an insect (bee/wasp) sting.

Transcript confirms sting was on the arm a few minutes ago with slight redness and a puncture mark and no particular swelling: "Yeah, it was on my arm... It's slightly red... there's a bit of a... hole..." and "It doesn't feel like particularly swollen." The side (right arm) is not specified, and "erythematous" is an added term but acceptable; however, specifying "right arm" is not supported.

Patient reports current breathing difficulty and anxiety about worsening: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment" and later "I don't feel like it's like particularly acute, but I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse." There is no mention of a distinct earlier brief episode of shortness of breath that has since improved; describing it as "brief earlier" is additional.
Patient explicitly expresses anxiety about progression: "I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse."
When asked about illnesses, patient says: "I've had eczema before. That's kind of the major thing."

Patient confirms episodic anxiety without medication: "Can I ask, do you suffer from anxiety or panic attacks... ?" "Yeah, sometimes. Occasionally." and "Have you ever been on medication for that?" "No. No."
Transcript states: "I'm allergic to penicillin." No description of the reaction (e.g., rash) is provided. Adding that it "causes a rash" is not supported.
Patient denies pet and food allergies: "Not that I know of. Yeah, I've been around dogs and cats." and "And you've got no food allergies as far as you're aware?" "No."
Patient states: "I am a computer scientist."
When asked if living alone, patient replies: "Yes."
Patient confirms having a cat: "Do you have any pets at home?" "I have a cat."

Clinician comments on normal appearance and speech: "based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing... I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction," indicating patient is conversing normally and not in visible distress.

Clinician notes normal lips/oral exam and no stridor: "your lips don't seem swollen to me right now" and after mouth/throat inspection: "Thankfully, I can't see any of that right now" and "Thankfully you don't have anything like that right now" in reference to stridor and airway compromise.

Clinician remarks on breathing appearing normal: "Your breathing seems all right to me right now" and later includes breathing in overall normal assessment, consistent with unlabored breathing on video.

Transcript describes the arm: "Yeah, it was on my arm... It's slightly red... there's a bit of a... puncture mark... Not particularly [swelling]. I guess it's just a bit kind of blotchy and a bit of a rash. It doesn't feel like particularly swollen." Warmth is not addressed, and arm side (right) is not specified. Claim of no warmth and specifying right arm are additions.

Clinician summarizes: "It seems to me that this is a localized allergic reaction" and notes absence of systemic features such as airway compromise: "I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction" and no swelling/stridor currently.

Patient links anxiety to the sting event: describes anxiety about breathing and swelling following the sting and says they "just wanted to speak to someone" about it. Clinician also acknowledges: "I can understand it is quite anxiety provoking." This supports anxiety secondary to the event.

Clinician advises: "you can get pyritone or chlorphenamine and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day. Okay? Or you can just take a one a day." This aligns with chlorphenamine 4 mg every 4–6 hours as needed or a daily alternative antihistamine.

Clinician educates on signs and actions but does not mention calling 999: "if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae... in some cases... it's better to go straight to AE..." There is no instruction to call 999; specifying this is beyond the transcript and conflicts with the documented advice route.

Clinician advises monitoring for spreading erythema/heat and possible infection: "If the redness in your arm spreads and it feels hot or, you know, you have signs of any localised infection, we may need to think about other treatments like an antibiotic." This matches monitoring for possible cellulitis requiring antibiotics.

Clinician states: "I'm going to leave some information about anaphylactic reactions just for you to read about it. I don't want you to panic, but just for you to be aware what symptoms are if those kind of things happen." and reassures about timing: "Given that it hasn't happened initially, it's unlikely to happen later... we may be coming out of the danger zone now." This supports written info and reassurance about low risk of delayed reaction.

Clinician advises re-contact/urgent care if worse: "however, if anything changes, if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae" and later "Get back to us if you're feeling worried. Just have a low threshold for having a chat with us." This is equivalent to re-contacting GP/Babylon or attending A&E if symptoms worsen.
